paras: The Appomattox mob of 1888 was the seizure and threatened lynching of Gen. T. T. (Thomas) Taylor and Col. J. A. Grayson, of Hutchinson, by armed residents of Appomattox, Grant County, Kansas, after the town lost a county-seat election to Ulysses in October 1888.
Accused of selling the town out, the two men were held under guard, threatened with hanging and made to sign over deeds and checks before they got away unharmed.
Papers across the country carried it as a county-seat election that nearly ended in a lynching.

Ulysses was reported to have beaten Appomattox, Golden, Shockeyville and Spurgeon with a clear majority of 2,150. Taylor was president of the Appomattox Town Company and Grayson its secretary, and a Topeka dispatch described Taylor as a legislator and a prominent candidate for governor at the last Republican convention. According to Grayson, the two town companies had agreed to a $10,000 forfeit if either used money in the election, and about 3 o'clock on election day the Ulysses side was alleged to have begun buying votes. The Topeka version instead said Appomattox people believed the two had traded the town's interests for lots in the winning town.

Appomattox men seized Taylor and Grayson and put them under guard, and "threats of lynching were freely made," Grayson told a Garden City reporter. The Topeka account said about a hundred heavily armed men made the two surrender at pistol point at the Appomattox hotel and handled them "very roughly." The captors made them assign the Ulysses agreement to the mob's leaders, give warranty deeds to all their property, sign checks for about $60,000 and write out an acknowledgment that they acted of their own free will.

The Kansas City wire said the sheriff and an armed posse arrived and rescued them, while Grayson's account had them leave at night under the guard of nine friends for a train at Hartland. The Topeka dispatch said they were held two days, until friends posing as a mob drew off the guards and the two climbed out an upper window to a carriage bound for Loken, the nearest railroad point.

Payment on the checks was stopped by telegraph and proceedings were planned to set aside the deeds, and Grayson said they considered themselves "lucky to have escaped with sound necks." An Appomattox mob was reported to be heading for Ulysses to collect the $10,000 forfeit, and another county-seat war was feared. On Oct. 19 Taylor asked Judge Abbott at Lakin to enjoin the canvass of the vote on behalf of Appomattox, but the application was denied, and that report added that no further violence had occurred. No arrests or charges against the captors appear in the coverage.

The Kansas City wire ran from Oct. 19 under headlines such as "Two Men in Danger of Lynching" in the Washington Evening Star, "Bleeding Kansas" in the Sacramento Record-Union and "Lively County Affairs" in the Richmond Dispatch. The Camden Evening Telegram played it as regional color, "A Way They Have in Kansas," and the Middleburgh Post headed it "Saved by a Posse" while placing Grant County in Missouri.

Kansas weeklies printed a fuller Garden City dispatch built on Grayson's statement, writing with some irony of deeds signed at the "request" of the captors. A later Topeka dispatch recast the story around Taylor, headlined "They Attempt to Lynch a Man Said to Have Betrayed Them" in Annapolis and "Narrow Escape From Lynching" in Richmond. By late October it had shrunk to one line in news-brief columns, and no article named the race of anyone involved.

The Kansas City and Garden City reports put the seizure on election day, a Tuesday, while the Topeka dispatch placed the election on "Friday last" and a Sacramento brief put the near-lynching "on Monday night." Grayson's presence in Garden City by Oct. 18 and Taylor's court application on Oct. 19 fit the Tuesday date best. Some Topeka copies named only Taylor and said he was jailed two days, while other accounts held both men at the hotel or under guard, and copies of the wire gave the checks as $60,000 or $80,000.

bases: Armed Appomattox residents seized two town-company officers, held them under guard and threatened to lynch them over a lost county-seat election; no one was killed (A1, A13, A20).
A mob (about a hundred armed men in one account) seized and threatened to hang Taylor and Grayson for supposedly selling the town out, but both escaped unharmed, so no one was killed (A13, A20, A21).
The Kansas City wire, a Garden City dispatch quoting Grayson, and a separate Topeka dispatch all report the seizure and lynching threats, though they differ on details (A1, A13, A20).

accounts.label: Grayson's statement (Garden City dispatch)
accounts.gist: The two were held under guard amid lynching threats, forced to sign over the agreement, deeds and $60,000 in checks, and left at night guarded by nine friends for a train at Hartland.

accounts.label: Topeka dispatch
accounts.gist: About a hundred armed men held Taylor (and Grayson) two days at the Appomattox hotel, or in one version jailed Taylor; friends got them away by carriage before a mob could act.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Kansas City wire as a curiosity of Kansas county-seat politics, under headlines like 'Two Men in Danger of Lynching' and 'A Way They Have in Kansas'.
Kansas weeklies printed Grayson's version with a wry tone, putting 'request' in quotation marks for the forced signatures.
The Topeka dispatch centered the 'thrilling and starling experience' of a prominent politician, headed 'They Attempt to Lynch a Man Said to Have Betrayed Them'.
